items.title: Another odd product
items.prose: Claim: $(2j + 1)(2k + 3)$ is odd for all integers $j$ and $k$. Expanding gives $4jk + 6j + 2k + 3$.
items.question: $4jk + 6j + 2k + 3 = 2(\ \square\ ) + 1$. What goes in the bracket?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write 3 as $2 + 1$, then take out the factor 2.

byKey.noone: You took out only $4jk + 6j + 2k$. The 3 also gives a 2 to the bracket.
byKey.nohalf: You did not halve the terms.

explain.text: $4jk + 6j + 2k + 3 = (4jk + 6j + 2k + 2) + 1 = 2(2jk + 3j + k + 1) + 1$. The bracket is an integer. So the product is odd.

items.title: Spot the slip
items.prose: A proof that odd times odd is odd.
items.question: Tap the line that breaks the proof.

feedback.correct: Right. One $k$ for both numbers covers only $a = b$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at how the two numbers are written.

byKey.r3: Line 4 follows from line 3. The fault is earlier.

explain.text: Line 2 writes both numbers with the same $k$. So it proves only that an odd number squared is odd. $3 \times 5$ is never covered. The fix is $a = 2j + 1$ and $b = 2k + 1$.

items.title: The contrapositive
items.prose: Claim: if $n^2 + 1$ is even then $n$ is odd.
items.question: Which statement should we prove instead?

options.text: If $n$ is even then $n^2 + 1$ is odd.
If $n$ is odd then $n^2 + 1$ is even.
options.why: You swapped the parts without negating them. That is the converse.

options.text: If $n^2 + 1$ is odd then $n$ is even.
options.why: You negated without swapping. That is the inverse.

options.text: If $n$ is even then $n^2 + 1$ is even.

feedback.correct: Right. Negate both parts and swap them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The contrapositive of $P \Rightarrow Q$ is $\lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P$.

explain.text: Not "$n$ is odd" is "$n$ is even", and it becomes the hypothesis. With $n = 2k$, $n^2 + 1 = 2(2k^2) + 1$, which is odd. That proves the claim.

items.title: Lowest terms for free
items.prose: The $\sqrt{2}$ proof begins: suppose $\sqrt{2} = \tfrac{p}{q}$ **in lowest terms**.
items.question: Why is it fair to assume lowest terms?

options.text: Every fraction can be cancelled to lowest terms, so the assumption costs nothing.
All fractions are already in lowest terms.
options.why: $\tfrac{4}{2}$ is not. But it cancels to $\tfrac{2}{1}$.

options.text: It is a rule that proofs must use lowest terms.
options.why: There is no such rule. It is allowed because any fraction can be cancelled.

options.text: It is not fair, so the proof has a gap.
options.why: It is fair: if $\sqrt{2}$ were any fraction, it would equal one in lowest terms.

feedback.correct: Right. If $\sqrt{2}$ were a fraction, it would be one in lowest terms.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether any fraction can be put in lowest terms.

explain.text: Divide $p$ and $q$ by their common factors until none is left. So a fraction equal to $\sqrt{2}$ gives one in lowest terms. The contradiction then needs that assumption.

items.title: Where to start
items.prose: Claim: $n! > 2^n$ for every $n$ from some point on. Here $n! = 1 \times 2 \times \dots \times n$.
items.question: What is the smallest $n$ for which $n! > 2^n$?

feedback.correct: Right. $4! = 24 > 16 = 2^4$, and the step keeps it going.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $n!$ and $2^n$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, 4$.

explain.text: $1 < 2$, $2 < 4$, $6 < 8$, then $24 > 16$. So the base case is $n = 4$. The step $(k + 1)! = (k + 1)\,k! > 2 \cdot 2^k$ works since $k + 1 > 2$.

items.title: A step in base 3
items.prose: Claim: $1 + 3 + 9 + \dots + 3^{n-1} = \tfrac{3^n - 1}{2}$. Step: assume the sum to $k$ terms is $\tfrac{3^k - 1}{2}$, then add $3^k$.
items.question: $\dfrac{3^k - 1}{2} + 3^k = \dfrac{\square}{2}$. What is the numerator?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $3^k$ as $\tfrac{2 \cdot 3^k}{2}$ first.

byKey.two: You added $3^k$ to the numerator without doubling it. Over 2, it is $2 \cdot 3^k$.

explain.text: $\tfrac{3^k - 1}{2} + \tfrac{2 \cdot 3^k}{2} = \tfrac{3 \cdot 3^k - 1}{2} = \tfrac{3^{k+1} - 1}{2}$. That is the formula for $k + 1$ terms. With the base case $1 = \tfrac{3 - 1}{2}$, induction proves it.

items.title: Refuting an implication
items.prose: Claim: for every integer $n$, if $n^2 > 4$ then $n > 2$.
items.question: Which integer is a counterexample?

options.why: $1^2 = 1$ is not above 4, so the hypothesis fails. 1 refutes nothing.
$9 > 4$ and $3 > 2$. It agrees with the claim.
$(-2)^2 = 4$, which is not greater than 4. The hypothesis fails.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find an integer with $n^2 > 4$ and $n \le 2$.

explain.text: A counterexample needs the hypothesis true and the conclusion false. $-3$ has $(-3)^2 = 9 > 4$ and $-3 \le 2$. Every $n \le -3$ works.

items.title: A root that is not one
items.prose: A student solves $\sqrt{x + 6} = x$ by squaring: $x + 6 = x^2$, so $(x - 3)(x + 2) = 0$, so $x = 3$ or $x = -2$.
items.question: Which is right?

options.text: Only $x = 3$ works. Squaring does not reverse, and $\sqrt{4} = 2 \ne -2$.
Both work, since each solves $x + 6 = x^2$.
options.why: You trusted the squared equation. Squaring can add solutions, so check each one in the original.

feedback.correct: Right. Squaring works forwards only, so each answer must be checked.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put each answer back into $\sqrt{x + 6} = x$.

explain.text: The chain $\sqrt{x + 6} = x \Rightarrow x + 6 = x^2$ runs one way only. $x = -2$ solves the squared equation but gives $\sqrt{4} = 2 \ne -2$. A step that does not reverse can add false answers.

items.title: Choosing the method
items.prose: Claim: if $n^2$ is a multiple of 3 then $n$ is a multiple of 3.
items.question: Which method fits best?

options.text: Contrapositive: if $n$ is not a multiple of 3, show $n^2$ is not.

options.why: You took the direct route. A square root shows no factor of 3, as with $\sqrt{2m}$.
The claim is true, so no counterexample exists.
Knowing the claim for $n$ says little about $n + 1$ here. Turn it round instead.

feedback.correct: Right. The hypothesis is about $n^2$, so turn it round.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which statement starts from something about $n$ itself.

explain.text: If $n = 3m + 1$ or $3m + 2$, then $n^2 = 3(3m^2 + 2m) + 1$ or $3(3m^2 + 4m + 1) + 1$. Neither is a multiple of 3. That is the contrapositive, so the claim holds.
